items.title: Mike Tyson: Power, Discipline, and Reinvention
items.style: Write an original English documentary narration with ten connected sections, each about 200 words, totaling 2,000 words. Use each segment source only for its stated facts. Do not invent dates, statistics, fight results, quotations, motives, private thoughts, or causal claims. Treat the five visual people as Mike Tyson, Cus D’Amato, Muhammad Ali, Sugar Ray Robinson, and Joe Frazier. The last three are historical reference points only: never claim they fought, coached, or directly influenced Tyson. Each segment source includes the one original editorial overlay line assigned to that segment. Include that line once, verbatim, in its section; do not use another section’s assigned line. These are narrator captions, not Mike Tyson quotations. Give the full story chronological flow, with an engaging opening and reflective close. Be specific, balanced, accurate, and sober about the conviction and legal accountability. Avoid generic motivational filler and graphic or sensational detail. English only.

source.topic: Mike Tyson's boxing life: discipline, championship, adversity, and reinvention
source.source_text: Factual source notes for an original documentary narration. Mike Tyson was born in Brooklyn, New York, on June 30, 1966. As a teenager he met Bobby Stewart, a counselor and former boxer, who introduced him to trainer Cus D'Amato. D'Amato became Tyson's coach and legal guardian. Tyson won Junior Olympic gold medals in 1981 and 1982. He made his professional debut on March 6, 1985, and won his first 19 professional bouts by knockout. D'Amato died on November 4, 1985, before Tyson won a world heavyweight title. On November 22, 1986, Tyson defeated Trevor Berbick for the WBC heavyweight title at age 20, becoming the youngest heavyweight champion in boxing history. He won the WBA title in 1987 and later that year unified the WBC, WBA, and IBF heavyweight titles by defeating Tony Tucker. His first professional defeat came against James 'Buster' Douglas in Tokyo in 1990. In 1992 Tyson was convicted of rape in Indiana and received a prison sentence; he was released on parole in 1995. He returned to boxing and regained the WBC and WBA titles in 1996. He lost the WBA title to Evander Holyfield later in 1996. In their 1997 rematch Tyson was disqualified after biting Holyfield's ears; the Nevada commission revoked his boxing license, which was later restored. Tyson was knocked out by Lennox Lewis in 2002. His professional record at the end of 2005 was reported as 50 wins, 6 losses, 2 no contests, and 44 knockouts. Muhammad Ali, Sugar Ray Robinson, and Joe Frazier are major historical figures in boxing and may be used only as contextual reference points, not as people who fought or coached Tyson. A balanced account should distinguish athletic achievement from personal harm and legal accountability, avoid treating conviction as an allegation, avoid inventing direct quotes, and avoid claiming that boxing outcomes alone define a person's whole life. Five people are image targets: Mike Tyson, Cus D'Amato, Muhammad Ali, Sugar Ray Robinson, and Joe Frazier.

segments.topic: Amateur success and the 1985 professional debut
segments.source_text:

Describe the transition from amateur competition to paid professional boxing using only these facts and the relationship with trainer Cus D’Amato. Do not invent training routines, private thoughts, or dialogue.

Cus D’Amato remained his trainer during this early period.

segments.source_text:
Cus D’Amato died on November 4, 1985, before Tyson won a world heavyweight title. Keep the chronology clear. Discuss how the facts mark a change in Tyson’s career story without inventing what either man privately thought or claiming an unsupported causal effect on later results.

Assigned editorial overlay line to include verbatim once: Footwork Creates the Opening.

segments.topic: The WBA, WBC, and IBF titles in 1987
segments.source_text:
Tyson won the WBA heavyweight title in 1987. Later that year he defeated Tony Tucker and unified the WBC, WBA, and IBF heavyweight titles. Describe the sequence precisely, explaining what unification means in boxing terms without adding unverified records or implying the titles made him unbeatable.

Assigned editorial overlay line to include verbatim once: Preparation Begins Long Before the Bell.

segments.topic: The first professional defeat in Tokyo
segments.source_text:
Tyson’s first professional defeat came against James “Buster” Douglas in Tokyo in 1990. Treat the loss as a documented result. Reflect on how a defeat can change a public narrative without inventing explanations, excuses, round-by-round details, or private motives.

Assigned editorial overlay line to include verbatim once: A Loss Exposes What Victory Can Hide.

segments.topic: The 1992 conviction and release on parole
segments.source_text:
In 1992 Tyson was convicted of rape in Indiana and received a prison sentence. He was released on parole in 1995. State the conviction accurately and soberly; do not frame it as an allegation, sensationalize it, describe graphic details, or let athletic achievements erase the harm and legal accountability.

Assigned editorial overlay line to include verbatim once: A Champion Is More Than a Record.

Tyson returned to boxing after his 1995 parole. He regained the WBC and WBA titles in 1996, then lost the WBA title to Evander Holyfield later that year. Describe both the comeback and the loss, without treating the return as proof that past harm was undone.

Assigned editorial overlay line to include verbatim once: Reinvention Is Part of the Fight.

segments.topic: The 1997 disqualification, later career, and legacy
segments.source_text:
In the 1997 rematch Tyson was disqualified after biting Holyfield’s ears. The Nevada commission revoked his boxing license and later restored it. Lennox Lewis knocked Tyson out in 2002. At the end of 2005 his reported professional record was 50 wins, 6 losses, 2 no contests, and 44 knockouts. Close by balancing sporting achievement, defeat, accountability, reinvention, and the fact that a record does not define a whole person.

Assigned editorial overlay line to include verbatim once: Legacy Outlasts the Final Round.
